entire trail — Manage trails across repositories and branches A trail captures project intent across repositories and branches. Manage intent and discussions on the whole trail; use --repo and --branch to select context for checkout, sessions, findings, and approvals. When to use this: Trail commands talk to entire.io and read the saved login from the OS keyring (the Keychain on macOS), so they need network and keyring access. If you run commands in a sandbox, request unsandboxed execution for `entire trail` up front. An error saying the Keychain is not accessible or the network is not allowed means the sandbox blocked it, not that the user is logged out: ask to re-run it unsandboxed, and do not run `entire login`. A project trail spans repositories; each change is its branch in one repository. Project trails and changes are numbered separately: never pass

where a change is expected, or where a project trail is. Pass / to checkout, resume, finding, watch, approvals or approve; given to show, it shows the parent project trail. Users paste Entire trail URLs. Do not pass a URL to any command; map the path after the host to a selector: //-/trails/

/changes// change / ///-/trails/

/changes/ change / ///trails/ change / //-/trails/

project trail

Add --project / unless is origin's owner. To link a trail or change, use the url `entire trail show` prints. # The Entire Elements of Style

Apply these rules to any text you write or edit. Before returning a draft, run the checklist in section 5 against it. When a rule conflicts with your default habits (em dashes, bulleted summaries, closing recaps), the rule wins.

Source: `entirehq/Entire-Marketing`, `playbooks/entire-elements-of-style.md` at commit `f1f13092ffddc360def4a715ee816a5b52257ab5`.

---

*This is a style guide that every Entiron should use to guide their writing. Any diversions from the below rules will be treated as serious grammatical infractions.*

As you’ll see, this document is formatted using our style guide and can be used as a reference for written content. I also recommend feeding these rules to your agent of choice, so that your pre-settings are aligned with our brand preferences.

## 1. Titles and Headings Use Title Case

At Entire, we follow the [Chicago Manual of Style](https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/home.html) in our published content. This means that titles and headings should be written in title case, with each word besides articles, conjunctions, and prepositions capitalized.

Always run your titles and top-level headings through the [Title Case checker to be safe](https://capitalizemytitle.com/).

### 1.1 Subheadings Also Use Title Case

Any further subheadings beyond this level (which we ought to avoid for clarity’s sake) may be written in sentence case.

## 2. Grammatical Rules and Preferences

Our style acts as our first impression to the world. It dictates how we will be perceived and evaluated by developers. Therefore, we strive for clarity, consistency, and concision through the grammatical rules detailed below.

### 2.1 Active Voice

We write in active voice. In practice, this means that each sentence contains a subject and a verb, and that the subject performs the action in the sentence.

For example, these sentences are in active voice:

* *Developers write code.*
* *We shipped a new search capability.*
* *I will be at the Barcelona hackathon this weekend.*

These sentences are written in passive voice and should be avoided:

* *The code is written by developers.*
* *A new feature has been added to our CLI.*
* *The hackathon will be hosted by Entire.*

Exceptions apply in very limited cases; for example, press releases.

### 2.2 The Oxford Comma

We use the Oxford comma in lists of three or more items, consistent with the Chicago Manual of Style preferences.

For example, if we wanted to write a sentence about Marvin’s plans for the day, we would style it: *Marvin planned to mope, moan, and pout.*

If we styled the sentence: *Marvin planned to mope, moan and pout,* we imply that the final two items in the list are combined into a single activity, “moan and pout.”

Note that when two parts of a sentence are combined with “and,” there is sometimes a comma and sometimes not. More [here](https://www.grammarly.com/blog/punctuation-capitalization/comma-before-and/).

### 2.3 Goodbye, Em Dash and En Dash

Though the em dash (—) and its shorter brother, the en dash (–), are punctuation options consistent with the Chicago Manual of Style, we make a conscious departure here and strike these dashes from our content.

This is both a preference of our CEO and an effort to deter accusations of “AI slop.”

The hyphen (-) is allowed when math is involved (as a minus sign), when we show code, or when it is part of a product name, e.g. git-sync.

### 2.4 Citation Style

We [hyperlink](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/294830/the-elements-of-style-illustrated-by-strunk-white-kalman/) citations in-text, another departure from Chicago Style for ease of reading.

## 3. The Case Against AI Slop

We understand that Entirons will use AI to write early drafts of their work. However, we expect them to respect their readers and themselves by striking these signs of slop from their writing.

### 3.1 Unnecessary Lists of Three (and Lists in General)

They’re annoying, silly, and meaningless. Only use lists when appropriate, including bulleted ones, which AI agents often assemble from illogical items.

* A list
* Only makes sense
* When it’s made up of parallel additions
* Unlike this one

### 3.2 Negative Parallelism

It’s not just fluff, it’s bullshit. And unless the terms being negated are actually opposites, it doesn’t make sense.

For example, a negative parallelism might read: *It’s not just redundant, it’s repetitive.*

And could be rephrased to say: *It’s redundant*.

### 3.3 Obscuring the Point

AI drafts routinely spend a paragraph approaching the thing they want to say. We cut throat-clearing opening sentences that talk around the idea.

Common examples include: *In today's rapidly evolving..., As AI continues to..., It's worth noting..., Importantly..., In many ways..., The reality is..., When it comes to…*

When background is necessary, it can come after. But we should always lead with the point.

### 3.4 Rowing the Boat

Agents write sentences that are easy to read, but hard to understand from a distance. Do you ever read a long draft from Claude and think, *Okay, I understand all the sentences in that paragraph. But did they actually mean anything new next to one another?*

This is why we should avoid what I’d like to call “rowing the boat,” or sentences that just go through the motions. Try reading your draft out loud and see if you’d actually say each sentence. Then you’ll find great examples of unnecessary fluff to cut.

Every sentence in a paragraph should be unique, and every paragraph should further the argument.

### 3.5 Forced Conclusions

AI-generated drafts often use a summary in place of a conclusion. Once you’ve made your point, no need to restate it at the end.

## 4. A Note on Substance

Though this guide is focused on style, a few final notes on substance.

### 4.1 Know Your Audience

Assume the reader is technically sophisticated. Don't explain concepts they are likely to know (Git, commits, branches, repositories, CLIs, APIs, or other common terms) unless the explanation is necessary to the point being made. Write as one practitioner talking to another.

### 4.2 Evidence Over Adjective

To that end, when possible, choose evidence over the empty promises of adjectives and hyperbole like “seamless,” “fast,” “powerful,” or “supercharged.” Specificity is important; if you can name the action, name it.

For example, developers don't *leverage our context capabilities to enhance workflows.* They *search previous agent sessions.*

### 4.3 Avoid Absolutes

We also *always* (😉) avoid absolute terms like “always,” “never,” “everything,” and “permanent,” unless categorically true.

### 4.4 You vs. We

Think critically about perspective. In our public-facing materials, “we” means Entirons, while “you” means the developer using the product. They are not interchangeable.

### 4.5 Show, Don’t Tell

When in doubt, “show, don’t tell,” is a useful paradigm. It’s cliched for a reason!

## 5. Final Instructions for Agents

Before returning a draft, prompt your agent to:

*Remove throat-clearing, unnecessary summaries, gratuitous lists, negative parallelism, em and en dashes, unsupported superlatives, repeated conclusions, and sentences that don't add information. Replace abstract marketing language with concrete descriptions. Preserve technical terminology exactly. Do not invent facts, product behavior, commands, examples, customer claims, or capabilities. Do not rewrite technically precise language merely for stylistic variety.*

The overall order of priorities for both humans and agents is as follows:

*Accuracy → substance → clarity → concision → voice → cleverness*

When two goals conflict, the one further to the left wins. Never sacrifice technical accuracy for a cleaner sentence, or substance for a clever line, though, of course, we’re all very clever. 🤓

For a repository whose `origin` uses the `entire://` scheme, the view lists the sessions as entire.com does: every session on every branch, under the name Entire gave it, with the checkpoints Entire lists for it. CONTRIBUTING.md:74:**Open VSX.** The steps are in the [Open VSX publishing guide](https://github.com/eclipse/openvsx/wiki/Publishing-Extensions).
CONTRIBUTING.md:76:1. Create an Eclipse account, sign in to open-vsx.org with GitHub, and accept the Publisher Agreement in the profile settings.
CONTRIBUTING.md:77:2. Generate an access token under Settings, Access Tokens, and create the namespace with `npx ovsx create-namespace entire -p <token>`.
CONTRIBUTING.md:78:3. Save the token as the secret `OVSX_PAT` in the repository's `open-vsx` environment.
CONTRIBUTING.md:80:The two publish jobs run in the `marketplace` and `open-vsx` environments. Add required reviewers to them in the repository settings if a release should wait for an approval.
README.md:3:Browse the [Entire](https://entire.com) checkpoints behind your commits, the agent sessions behind each checkpoint, and the trails of a repository on entire.com, in the editor where you read the code.
README.md:11:**Sessions view.** Lists the sessions running now, then the rest by recency, each with its checkpoints under it. ## Screenshots

The two pictures in `images/` are of the extension in VS Code, on a demo repository with made-up commits, sessions, and trails. The fake Entire CLI in `test/fake-entire` supplies the data, as it does for the extension-host tests. Retake them when a view changes, and take them from made-up data: a screenshot of a real repository publishes its session names, prompts, and transcripts.

The README links to them by relative path. `vsce` rewrites those links to this repository on GitHub when it packages the extension, so the pictures are not in the VSIX, and they show on the Marketplace only while the repository is public.

## Releasing

A release is a tag. Pushing `v<version>` runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which builds the VSIX once and publishes that one file to the Visual Studio Marketplace, to Open VSX, and to a GitHub release for the tag. The release takes its notes from the version's entry in `CHANGELOG.md`, and its VSIX is the file to install by hand with Extensions: Install from VSIX.

1. Update `version` in `package.json` and add an entry to `CHANGELOG.md`.
2. Run `npm run check`, `npm run test:host`, and `npm run package`. The last command writes `entire-<version>.vsix`.
3. Install that file with `code --install-extension entire-<version>.vsix` and open a repository that has checkpoints.
4. Commit, then tag and push the tag: `git tag v<version>` and `git push origin v<version>`.

### One-Time Setup

**Visual Studio Marketplace.** The workflow signs in with [GitHub Trusted Publishing](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/working-with-extensions/publishing-extension), so the repository stores no Marketplace token. The personal access tokens that `vsce` used before are retired on December 1, 2026.

1. Create the publisher `entire` at [marketplace.visualstudio.com/manage](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/manage). Its ID has to match `publisher` in `package.json`, and it cannot be changed later.
2. Open the publisher, select Trusted Publishing, and create a policy with repository owner `entireio`, repository `entire-vscode`, workflow `release.yml`, and environment `marketplace`.

**Open VSX.** The steps are in the [Open VSX publishing guide](https://github.com/eclipse/openvsx/wiki/Publishing-Extensions).

1. Create an Eclipse account, sign in to open-vsx.org with GitHub, and accept the Publisher Agreement in the profile settings.
2. Generate an access token under Settings, Access Tokens, and create the namespace with `npx ovsx create-namespace entire -p <token>`.
3. Save the token as the secret `OVSX_PAT` in the repository's `open-vsx` environment.

The two publish jobs run in the `marketplace` and `open-vsx` environments. Add required reviewers to them in the repository settings if a release should wait for an approval.
--- release.yml (origin/main) ---
name: Release

# Push a tag named v<version> to build the extension once and publish that one
# file to the Visual Studio Marketplace, to Open VSX, and to a GitHub release for
# the tag.
#
# Marketplace: GitHub Trusted Publishing, so no secret is stored. The publisher
# needs a Trusted Publishing policy that names this repository, this workflow
# file (release.yml), and the environment "marketplace".
#
# Open VSX: the OVSX_PAT secret, an access token from open-vsx.org.
#
# CONTRIBUTING.md has the one-time setup for both.

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - 'v*'

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - name: Check that the tag matches package.json
        run: |
          version="$(node -p "require('./package.json').version")"
          if [ "v${version}" != "${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" ]; then
            echo "Tag ${GITHUB_REF_NAME} does not match package.json version ${version}." >&2
            exit 1
          fi
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run check
      - run: npm run notices -- --check
      - run: xvfb-run -a npm run test:host
      - run: npm run package
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: entire-vscode-vsix
          path: '*.vsix'
          if-no-files-found: error

  github-release:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      # Lets the job create the release and upload the VSIX to it.
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: entire-vscode-vsix
      - name: Attach the VSIX to the release for the tag
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          version="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          # The release notes are the CHANGELOG.md entry for this version.
          awk -v heading="## ${version}" '$0 == heading { found = 1; next } found && /^## / { exit } found' CHANGELOG.md > notes.md
          if gh release view "${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
            gh release upload "${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" entire-*.vsix --clobber
          else
            gh release create "${GITHUB_REF_NAME}" entire-*.vsix --verify-tag --title "Entire for VS Code ${version}" --notes-file notes.md
          fi

  publish-marketplace:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: marketplace
    permissions:
      contents: read
      # Lets the job ask GitHub for the short-lived token that the Marketplace exchanges.
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: entire-vscode-vsix
      - run: npx vsce publish --oidc --packagePath entire-*.vsix

  publish-open-vsx:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: open-vsx
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: entire-vscode-vsix
      - run: npx ovsx publish entire-*.vsix
        env:
          OVSX_PAT: ${{ secrets.OVSX_PAT }}

# Changelog

## 0.1.0

Initial release.

- Checkpoints view that lists each commit on the current branch with an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, including commits that carry several checkpoints and checkpoints that no commit on the branch carries.
- Sessions view that merges running sessions, local session state, and sessions referenced by checkpoints, each with its checkpoints under it. For a repository whose `origin` uses the `entire://` scheme, the view lists the sessions as entire.com does: every session on every branch, under the name Entire gave it, with the checkpoints Entire lists for it. In any other repository, each session is named by the prompt that opened it.
- Detail panel with the commit, the files touched with diffs, and a transcript whose tool calls expand to show their input and result. Each prompt in the transcript names the person who sent it.
- Each checkpoint's place in its session, such as 12 of 249, on its row and in the detail panel, with Previous and Next to step through the session. The selected row in the sidebar moves to the checkpoint the tab steps to.
- A checkpoint whose session data was never uploaded opens on its commit and diff, with a note that says why there is no transcript.
- Open on entire.com for commits, sessions, and trails in repositories whose `origin` uses the `entire://` scheme.
- Trails view for those repositories, which lists the trails that touch the repository and marks the trail on the checked-out branch. A filter shows only the trails in one state: all, open, closed, or an open trail's phase of planning, building, or complete. The `entire.trails.enabled` setting turns trails off.
- Trail panel with the trail's description, the merge gates and CI runs of each change, and a timeline whose commits open their checkpoints. The panel draws the trail's title at once and fills in the changes and the timeline as the Entire CLI returns them. A trail opened earlier in the same window shows from that read while the panel reads it again.
- Brain view, collapsed until you open it, with what the entire-brain plugin reports about the repository's brain. Its View Brain button starts the plugin's graph page for the repository and opens it in the browser.
- Open Raw Transcript for the stored transcript in the agent's own format.
- Lists that show 50 rows at a time and load the next 50 when you scroll to the end, with a Load More row to click as well. The extension reads further back in the commit history only when a page needs it.
